body:
Triage: labelled `finding` (observation, awaiting first-touch grading) — the performance budget's blind spot is a gauge-design question (what the budget should weigh, and whether a per-chunk or aggregate ceiling is maintainable) rather than a named-landing-point defect; no user hits it today. Related: #5325 (the ineffective lazy imports are one concrete contributor to the statically-pulled weight this budget cannot see) — grade the pair together.

---
_Generated by [Claude Code](https://claude.ai/code)_

Triage first-touch grading (finding centralized round, 2026-08-20, triage seat session `session_016A4EBi3ky1mjTi6vD2kCvA`): **promote to `pm:queue`**, type Task, paired with #5325 (one lane slot, #5325 is the concrete half). Re-verified on `origin/main`: `performance-budget.yml` still gzips a single `index-*.js` (~2.8% of the eager payload) against the 350 KB budget — the #5266 89 KiB regression landed in a vendor chunk and was structurally invisible to this gauge. Direction already converged on the card: ratchet the eager import closure against `main` rather than absolute-threshold the entry chunk.

Full evidence posted on #5325.",

Which route should the card take? (I did not pick one; packages/fields is untouched in PR #5466.)",
      "options": [
        "A. Chunking first, then the barrel. Stop `ui-components` from claiming packages/fields (or split fields into its own group), then remove the defeating static re-exports. The ONLY order in which the barrel work moves bytes. Cost: a bundling change needing its own measurement — that group exists to stop chunk explosion, and fields widgets are reached from many places — plus the same breaking API change to @object-ui/fields and a refactor of 4 production modules across 3 packages.",
        "B. Delete the decorative laziness. Honest and cheap: no bytes claimed, no false signal. Cost: it deletes getLazyFieldWidget, which is public API and is used by app-shell's ActionParamDialog, so it is also a breaking change — and it forecloses A.",
        "C. Leave the code, kill the noise. Cheapest; buys nothing. Cost: the 43 warnings keep scrolling past in every build, which is exactly the signal-erosion half the card objects to.",
        "D. Close #5325 as measured-and-not-worth-it, and re-file the chunk-group question as its own card. Cost: the dead intent stays in the source with no marker on it."
      ],
      "recommendation": "A, but explicitly SEQUENCED and not before the chunking half is measured — and the sequencing is the recommendation, not the destination. Real business need: the closure is 3.79 MB gzipped before first render, which is a real cost on every console page load for every user, so the underlying need is genuine — but the need is served by moving BYTES, and route B/C move none while A's first step is the only one that can. Nothing here should be started as barrel cleanup: that was measured at 0 bytes for a breaking change, which is the worst trade of the four. Long-term soundness: A is the only route that makes the declared intent (a lazy widget) and the emitted reality (an eager chunk) agree; B and C both resolve the contradiction by giving up the intent, and this is a renderer whose whole cost model is 'heavy widgets load when used'. A is also the route the #5324 gauge now makes checkable — before this PR nobody could have told which of the four moved bytes, which is how the intent stayed dead for so long. Making AI-written code hard to get wrong: the defect class is 'a declaration nothing enforces', and it has now cost twice (#5266, #5325). A ends with the declaration enforced by the eager-closure number itself; C leaves a dynamic import that silently does nothing, which is precisely the shape an AI author copies as a working pattern. The three axes conflict on cost, not direction: A is by far the most expensive and needs its own card and its own measurement, so if the startup-focus call is that this is not worth the engineering now, D (close as measured, re-file the chunk-group question) is the honest cheap answer — NOT C, which leaves the misleading source in place. Maintainer's call; the measurement is on #5325 either way."

      "question": "Should the eager-closure ceiling be TIGHTENED below today's payload, and on what schedule? Per the dispatch I landed a truthful current-state ceiling (3,960,000 bytes = today plus 2.02%) and did not lower it unilaterally. The gap is large and worth naming: 3.79 MB gzipped before first render is a bad payload, and the largest single eager chunk is vendor-objectstack at 1,493 KB (38% of the closure), followed by framework at 484 KB and ui-components at 380 KB.",
      "options": [
        "A. Leave the absolute ceiling and revisit after the closure is actually cleaved (e.g. after #5325 route A, or #5359). Simplest; the gate already catches a #5266-class regression today.",
        "B. Convert to a true ratchet against main (the direction triage originally converged on). Sharper, but it needs a main build per PR in CI, and two independently-green PRs can still combine to trip it in the merge queue.",
        "C. Add per-chunk budgets on top of the aggregate, so vendor-objectstack cannot grow unnoticed inside an aggregate that has headroom."
      ],
      "recommendation": "A now, C next, and B only if C proves insufficient. The shipped gate's headroom (78,391 bytes) is already narrower than the 89 KiB regression it exists to catch, so the marginal value of B over A today is small relative to its merge-queue cost — the queue rebuilds every PR on current main, so a strict ratchet turns any two concurrent size-adding PRs into a queue ejection neither author can see coming. C is the cheapest real tightening and targets where the mass actually is: one chunk holds 38% of the closure. All three are separate decisions from this PR, which is why none of them is in it."
